conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists on your care team. You're here today because of a kidney stone in your right ureter. We're going to get you ready for surgery tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, doctor. I’ve been having a lot of pain on my right side. Is that from the stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s very likely. The stone is blocking the tube that carries urine from your kidney to your bladder, which causes pain and can affect kidney function if not treated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. I’ve had stones before, but this one feels worse. What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow you’ll have a procedure called ureteroscopy. The urologist will go in through your bladder and use a laser to break up the stone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds intense. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very common and generally safe. But because you have a mechanical heart valve, we need to be careful with your blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I take Coumadin every day. I stopped it as they told me, but I’m worried about clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’re starting you on heparin today — an IV blood thinner — to protect your heart while we pause the Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I’m on heparin now instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Heparin works quickly and can be stopped right before surgery. After your procedure, we’ll restart Coumadin and overlap it with heparin until your INR is in the safe range — between 2.5 and 3.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely about a week. We’ll keep you until we’re sure the Coumadin is working and you’re recovering well from surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I just reviewed your labs. Your hemoglobin is a bit low at 11.2, but stable. White blood cells are normal, so no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the stone or something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be from minor bleeding related to the stone. You mentioned past guaiac-positive stools — we should keep an eye on that, but it’s not urgent now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My breathing feels a little tight, but I think it’s just from being anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. You have COPD, so we’ll make sure your inhalers are available. Use your albuterol as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your PTT was checked this morning — it’s 51.3, which is in range for heparin. Surgery is scheduled for noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? I’m nervous about the anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very normal to feel that way. The anesthesiologist will use general anesthesia, but they’ll monitor your heart and lungs closely. Your history of heart attack and COPD means extra caution, but you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had two strokes and heart surgery — I just want to get through this safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s exactly our goal. Your team knows your history well. We’ve coordinated with cardiology and anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. Thompson. You’re back from surgery. Everything went smoothly — the stone was broken up and a stent was placed in your ureter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. I feel groggy, but no pain yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. You’ll likely feel some flank discomfort or urgency to urinate because of the stent, but we’ll manage that with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to restart your Coumadin and make sure your INR climbs into the target range. That’ll take a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your post-op PTT came back at 97.7 — a bit high, but expected after heparin. We’ve adjusted the drip to keep it safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? High PTT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We monitor it closely. Right now, it’s within acceptable limits for your situation. We’re balancing bleeding risk with clot prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 163 yesterday — a bit high, but not concerning. We’ll keep monitoring it. Are you taking your diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been on glyburide and metformin for years. I try to watch my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re continuing those here. Your kidney function is normal — creatinine is 0.9 — so it’s safe to keep using them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve been urinating a little pink. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, light pink urine is common after this procedure. It’s from minor bleeding due to the stent. As long as it’s not bright red or clotted, it’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.1. We’re getting closer to the target of 2.5–3.5. We’ll keep the heparin running a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So once it hits 2.5, I can stop the IV and go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We’ll stop heparin when your INR is stable above 2.5. Then we’ll observe you for a day to make sure it stays up before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated since the surgery. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. Narcotics can slow your bowels. We’ll start docusate, a stool softener, to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I don’t want to be uncomfortable longer than I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news — your INR is 2.8 today. That’s in the target range. We’re stopping the heparin now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll watch your INR tomorrow to confirm it stays stable. If so, discharge is likely on the 25th.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a question about my Coumadin. I was taking 8mg most days, but 6mg on Tuesdays and Fridays. Should I go back to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We recommend resuming your home schedule: 8mg daily except Tuesdays and Fridays when you take 6mg. Your PCP or Coumadin nurse will monitor your INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried I’d forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR held at 2.7 today — stable. You’re on track for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the stent? When does that come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urologist will schedule that as an outpatient procedure in a week or two. It’s quick and done with a scope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my heart and blood pressure meds here — metoprolol, ramipril, furosemide. Should I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your home medications. You have diastolic heart failure and hypertension, so those are important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cholesterol meds — atorvastatin and ezetimibe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those. You have coronary disease, so keeping your LDL low is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’ll get a prescription for oxycodone for pain, but use it sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like taking narcotics. Can I switch to something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Talk to your PCP about alternatives. Just don’t drive or drink alcohol while on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What signs should I watch for after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor if you develop fever over 101.5, vomiting, or severe pain. Also watch for heavy bleeding or signs of clot — like chest pain or weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP within three days to check your INR. And schedule with your urologist for stent removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re medically cleared to go home. I’ve reviewed everything with you — any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand. Resume all my meds, watch for fever, and see my doctors soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You did well. Take care, and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — my feet have been itchy. Should I use that lotion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the camphor-menthol lotion is for your chronic skin condition. Use it as needed for itching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're all set. The nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember, call if you have chest pain — use the nitroglycerin and call 911.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I keep it with me always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll use the inhalers if I get short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re well prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for making sure I understood everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our job. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe journey home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.
